report.source_text: Serial MRI brain scans at presentation (A–C), 3 months (D–F) and 6 months (G–I) following initial presentation in a child with Baló’s concentric sclerosis. The initial MRI with contrast demonstrated a T2 hyperintense abnormality with central hypointense ring-like focus (A); alternating layers of high and low signal intensity giving it an ‘onion bulb’ appearance. There was central concentric contrast enhancement (B). At 3 months, the extent of the abnormality (D) and the area of contrast enhancement (E) had increased. At 6 months, the abnormality (G) and the contrast enhancement (H) had resolved. The abnormality showed central diffusion restriction with unrestricted diffusion in the periphery (C). The area of diffusion restriction increased in size at 3 months (F) and disappeared by 6 months (I).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A school-aged asymptomatic boy attended a routine optician appointment that raised concerns about papilloedema. Non-enhanced head CT demonstrated a well-demarcated hyperdense lesion in the left posterior frontal lobe with surrounding hypodensity (oedema). MRI brain revealed a lesion with alternating circular layers of high and low signal intensity giving an 'onion bulb' appearance consistent with Baló's concentric sclerosis, with central contrast enhancement and central diffusion restriction with unrestricted diffusion in the periphery. Repeat MRI at 3 months showed increase in size and change in signal characteristics, prompting a biopsy to exclude tumour. Histopathological examination confirmed a demyelinating inflammatory lesion. Serial MRI at 6 months demonstrated resolution of the abnormality and contrast enhancement, with disappearance of diffusion restriction. The patient remained asymptomatic throughout, was managed conservatively without treatment, and at 4-year follow-up remained stable and asymptomatic with further resolution of the lesion and no new lesions in the brain or spine.
